newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya government starts talks over air go-slow.
newsitem.headline: Kenya government starts talks over air go-slow.

text.p: Kenya's government on Monday started negotiations with air traffic controllers on the third day of a go-slow which has brought chaos to tourist and cargo flights, an airport official said.
The official said air traffic controllers were considering a government offer under which they would return to work and give the government two more weeks to consider their pay demand.
"The government's head of personnel met air traffic controllers on Monday afternoon and proposed a deal under which they would return to work," said the official, who declined to be identified.
Flights were delayed for up to 12 hours or diverted from Kenya's main airports on Monday.

An official at national carrier Kenya Airways said flights leaving Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport were delayed by between three and 12 hours and incoming flights were waiting up to two hours.

Kenya's air traffic controllers and staff at the meteorological office started a go-slow on Saturday complaining the government had failed to honour commitments it made to end a go-slow in December. They demand a 50-fold increase from what they said was pay of about $90 a month, plus benefits.
Tour operators, hotel managers and taxi drivers said they were losing business as a result of the go-slow which, like the December dispute, coincided with a busy tourist season.

"We get block bookings which are not taken up because passengers arrive late, and then tourists with no reservations get turned away even though the hotels aren't full," Boniface Righa of Sarova Hotels told Reuters.
Saudi Airlines, which had a flight delayed on Saturday for 24 -hours, said it had switched to using Boeing 747s from smaller Airbus planes because time was being wasted circling Nairobi airport.

"When a flight is delayed we lose money as we misconnect passengers and we have to endorse their tickets and you lose money when you endorse them. The total loss is tens of thousands of dollars," said Zein Shatry, duty officer with Saudi Airlines.

More than 200 tourists returning to Holland on an Air Holland charter from Mombasa, Kenya's second city and a tourism centre, were stranded at Moi International Airport on Monday after the pilot said his authorised flying hours had expired.
A row developed as passengers, forced to disembark and return to hotels, complained they risked losing their jobs.
Kenyan officials said the go-slow forced the postponement of a visit on Sunday by South African Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo.
Airports in Kisumu, Malindi and Nairobi's Wilson Airport were also affected by the go-slow.
An air traffic controller at Jomo Kenyatta airport said the situation there was "absolute chaos" with airlines running up high costs keeping tourists in hotels in Nairobi and Mombasa.
Jomo Kenyatta is the main cargo and passenger hub for East Africa and for some air cargo carriers is even more important than airports in South Africa, the continent's economic leader.
Air cargo giant Lufthansa Cargo said the go-slow could cost the industry millions of dollars if it continued much longer.
The go-slow increased pressure on a government hit by the International Monetary Fund on Thursday halting a $205 million aid package to Kenya, citing concern at high-level corruption.
Tourism is Kenya's largest single hard currency earner with 717,000 visitors in 1996.
